b: “I feel like people skip over the filmmaking sometimes,” laments writer-director Beth de Araújo. Discussion of her breakout feature, Josephine, has understandably centered on its harrowing inciting incident, which is drawn from the filmmaker’s own life: a brutal rape in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park, witnessed from a distance by the film’s eight-year-old title character (Mason Reeves). The moment is horrifyingly violating to watch, yet it’s only the first of many seismic shocks for the unsuspecting young girl and her parents.

What follows in Josephine is a chilling look at how social and legal systems struggle to process male violence, forcing others to bear its burdens. After the victim drops out of the state’s case, the assailant’s punishment rests entirely on Josephine’s testimony as the crime’s only other witness. But such a task requires more from the young girl than simply recounting what she saw. Despite the court’s best efforts to protect her, forcing Josephine to dwell on the rape risks retraumatizing her and exposing her to adult concepts she may be ill-equipped to comprehend.

Araújo charts, at once sensitively and searingly, Josephine’s path to the witness stand as she reckons with the fallout of what she saw. The film stays planted in its protagonist’s perspective while also showing how her parents’ competing philosophies shape that ever-evolving outlook. Her father, Damien (Channing Tatum), encourages a more confrontational, physical response that emphasizes self-protection. Her mother, Claire (Gemma Chan), instead urges introspection, hoping it will steer her daughter toward a sense of communal responsibility.

I spoke with Araújo ahead of Josephine’s theatrical release. Our conversation covered how she conveyed Josephine’s confusion through the camerawork, what it meant for the character to be strong, and why making the film changed her understanding of catharsis.

I’m a fellow sociology major, so I would love to know: How did that background inform Josephine? The film certainly lit up the parts of my brain that think about the socialization process, among other things.

When I first got to film school, I was like, “I feel so behind. Everyone knows every film under the sun and every person who worked on every film under the sun.” But now, I really do see it as a gift in the way I approach story and characters and how society has shaped them. I’ve always found the individual versus society such a fascinating concept. Certainly, society and everything around us influence who we are, how we think, and how we move through the world. I’m very grateful for that now. I do still love to read sociology books; they’re just so fascinating to me.

Society’s relationship to sexual assault both has and hasn’t changed a lot since you wrote the script. Did the film react to what was going on around it, or did it always stay true to a character’s experience that reflects your own?

I think it’s one and the same, actually. I think it’s a character reacting to something that’s around them, and unfortunately, rape is a global epidemic that’s really never been confronted by any society. Part of why I made this film was because I didn’t know where else to discuss it. I learned from quite an early age that people don’t talk about rape. It’s not something that’s welcome in any space. It’s a downer. It makes people uncomfortable. It’s inappropriate, so there’s just really no space for it. I want to give people that space.

Speaking of the ways in which it’s not discussed, there were obvious safety reasons for not talking directly with Mason about sexual assault. But was there also a thematic reason for reflecting that silence, and the difficulty of discussing the issue, in the very making of Josephine?

I always see the job of an artist as one of telling the truth as you see it and as you feel it, with no agenda. This is how I believe these characters, who live in a certain space and time, react to this subject matter. It was never a conscious choice to say, “I want to impart that rape is silenced in certain spaces.” That’s never how I approach a scene. It’s really: Who is this character? What have they experienced? How have they been socialized? How will they speak about this subject matter in this society? That’s how I approached it.

Since there are elements of Josephine drawn from your own life, how did you come to understand how the adults felt and responded? Was that informed by talking with your family or by your artistic imagination?

The truth of the matter was that I never spoke to my parents about it at all until about two decades later, so that isn’t a very interesting film. I have very particular parents who would maybe be a little bit alienating to an audience. I also think bringing them into the present day would make these parents a bit different from how mine parented in the ’90s, given how people have now been socialized to think about how you talk to your children and what’s appropriate. I felt like this was them trying their best. This is how they love their daughter.

I mainly thought about it from the perspective of how they each dealt with male violence in their own lives. The way Damien dealt with male violence as a kid was through male violence. He became the aggressor. That’s how he got it to stop. That’s his perspective on how to love and protect his daughter. His whole feeling is, “What are you going to do, talk a rapist to death? No, you’re gonna have to fucking fight him!” And then, with Claire’s character, the way she dealt with male violence was that she suppressed it, ran as far away from it as she could, and never talked about it. She didn’t want to let it define her or ruin her life, so she just kept moving. For her, that’s how she believes this won’t ruin Josephine’s life, even though, with a little more self-awareness, she knows that maybe she didn’t process it in the best way. That’s where they’re coming from, and that’s how I went about creating the idea of their parenthood.

There’s a phrase that became a bit of a punchline in the last decade when it comes to men speaking about sexual assault: “as the father of a daughter.” People love to criticize that preface because men should always be offended by sexual assault, not just when it could affect someone they love. How were you threading that needle with Damien, who has a real masculine nobility and strength but is also undeniably activated by male violence hitting so close to home?

There’s a certain kind of man who has traditional gender roles built into the way he sees the world and thinks about things. I think the way Damien sees Jo at the start of the film is, “This is my kid. This is neither a daughter nor a son. I’m raising my kid as I would raise a son.” This is the first time he has to think about the fact that she may not get as strong as he is, physically, and that terrifies him. That’s what awakens something in him: this recognition of the way her life could go. I think that, for better or worse, is the way some men start to understand gender.
What went into choosing the name Josephine? It’s a feminine name, but her nickname sounds more masculine.

That was part of choosing the name. I’m the second of four daughters, and Little Women is my mom’s favorite book, so Josephine felt appropriate. I did like how it could be shortened to Jo, which is what Damien always calls her.

Beyond the visual approach to the assault, how were you using the camera to bring the audience into the character’s subjective experience while also highlighting what she might not yet be equipped to understand?

I had long conversations with Greta Zozula, our cinematographer, about this. We knew we were going to use a direct POV for a couple of reasons. One, we knew we would never have the actress on set when we were shooting the sexual assault, and we needed to see it quite literally from her perspective. We decided to use this technique and make sure that it really felt like it was from the perspective of a child, transporting the audience back to feeling like they were eight years old again and lower to the ground. We then decided to use that direct POV whenever Josephine felt a little confused. If there was a sense of learning something for the first time, or wonder, or anything was coming at her anew, we would use that.

We were also making sure that even when we weren’t using that camera technique, we were in her perspective. Because, in a scene, power, perspective, and what you want to impart to the audience all shift every once in a while. But it was really important to us that the film felt heavy on top of this child—quite literally, from low angles. And, as she became more and more entangled in this mess, the frame became more chaotic.
Were you thinking about the film at all in relation to genre? I think it has elements of a coming-of-age movie, but it doesn’t reduce the experience to a lesson learned.

I never think about genre. I think about tone. I think about tone quite a lot, but I never try to impose a genre onto whatever it is that I’m doing. I just don’t find it helpful. I think about what I want the audience to feel in any given moment, how I can shift from one tonal scene to the next, and how that transition may play out emotionally for the audience. But I never really think, “Oh, this is horror. This is drama. This is a thriller.” This is just how I see a story.

With the film’s ending, deciding whether to frame Josephine’s story as an antihero’s journey or a hero’s journey was a real point of struggle for you. What ultimately broke the stalemate? Was it what you wanted to believe? What was right for the story? A little of both?

I had a meeting with a mentor at the Sundance Labs named Andrea Berloff, an incredible writer and filmmaker. When I was struggling with it, she said to me, “The beautiful thing about endings and about storytelling is that you can write whatever you want, and it doesn’t have to be true. It can be whatever you want.” And I thought, “Wow, how great would it be, though, if she just felt strong? If I felt strong?” That really helped me be like, “Well, I am still here. That has to stand for something in terms of my resilience dealing with this at quite a young age.” I really leaned into that, and then it became really clear to me what strength Damien was trying to impart to Josephine this whole time, and how she would then repurpose it.

In 2017, you told Filmmaker that “this film, in part, is a catharsis—a way of processing it as an adult who’s now getting closer to the age of that woman in the park.” Have you ultimately gotten that from this long journey with Josephine?

I think about catharsis in a different way now. For someone who witnesses a sexual assault or experiences sexual assault, I don’t think you ever heal fully. I think you become a different person: the person who can get through it. That’s certainly who I am and what’s happened. I heard a wonderful analogy for trauma the other day. There are quite a few, and I feel like trauma is quite an overused word sometimes in our culture. But it’s like a piece of glass that gets broken, and all of the glass shatters into different places. When you walk around, you occasionally step on different pieces where they landed. That resonates with me.

“Empowering” feels like a cheesy word, but I feel like maybe it is the right one for reclaiming a narrative about what you know is true in your experience. I think that’s amazing. I will say, this is the first year I have noticed that I am sleeping through the night, and that is huge for me. Whether or not it feels like a catharsis, something has changed and shifted in my body.
